name: Wrist-hand theory

lead: Wrist-hand theory is a looksmaxxing idea that the size of the wrists and hands reflects overall frame size, so thicker wrists and larger-looking hands make a person look broader and more imposing.

Proponents on looksmax.org discuss before-and-after photos of public figures and suggest the features can be modified, usually by invoking Wolff's law and bonesmashing. Little beyond forum discussion documents the idea.

paras: In the forum thread, the discussion centres on comparing photos and on bonesmashing hands and wrists, a practice of repeated impact aimed at stimulating bone remodeling. Grip and forearm training is a separate, conventional way people build thicker-looking forearms and wrists.
Repeated impact to the hands and wrists can cause fractures, ligament and nerve injuries. No published studies show that adult wrist or hand bone size can be increased this way.

chain: Impression of a bigger, sturdier frame
angle.text: Proponents argue that thick wrists and larger hands signal a robust frame and that this impression can be increased. The only route described in the source thread is bonesmashing.

lead: Wrist-hand theory is a framework discussed on looksmax.org holding that wrist and hand size reflect frame size and contribute to a strong, imposing appearance [1].

The main thread on the topic presents before-and-after photos of public figures, attributing differences to bonesmashing and Wolff's law, the principle that bone adapts to load. Replies in the thread are brief and partly joking in tone [1]. No clinical research on modifying wrist or hand bone size for appearance was found.

paras: The theory treats wrists and hands as visible indicators of skeletal frame size. A looksmax.org thread titled Wrist / Hand theory invites discussion of before-and-after photos of athletes, a singer and a rapper, claiming the changes reflect bone modification [1].

The original poster states the pictured changes are what bonesmashing on hands and wrists could achieve, at the reader's own risk, and cites Wolff's law as the rationale [1]. Replies call it a legitimate theory, with a sarcastic tone in places [1].

The thread itself notes the practice is at one's own risk [1]. Repeated striking of bones is generally associated with fractures and soft-tissue injury in the medical literature, though no study on this practice was found.

lore.intro: The idea appears on looksmax.org in a thread of before-and-after photo comparisons [1].

claims.claim: Hand and wrist size can be increased through bonesmashing, per Wolff's law
